gloss: bone; very, selfsame; be mighty, numerous; might
summary: עֶצֶם is a bone, and the bones as the frame and strength of the body, troubled in sickness and fear and refreshed by good news (Psa 6:3; Pro 15:30); “bone and flesh” is a man’s own kin (Gen 2:23; 2Sa 5:1). With “day” it marks the very day itself, בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, “on this selfsame day”, which fixes the feasts of Lev 23 to their day (Lev 23:14, 21, 28–30). The verb is to be strong and mighty, and so many, beyond counting (Exo 1:7; Psa 40:6), with עָצוּם “mighty, numerous” and nouns of might. Arabic ʿaẓm “bone” and ʿaẓuma “be great”, and Phoenician ʿṣm “bone” and ʿṣmt “great deed”, keep bone and might together in one root, as Hebrew does; the rare “shut the eyes” (Isa 29:10; 33:15) has no clear tie to either.

words.summary: A bone, a person’s or an animal’s, and the bones as the whole frame. From that it is the thing itself: “the bone of this day” is the very day, and “as the bone of the heavens” the heavens themselves. Its plural is mostly עֲצָמוֹת of a body’s bones, and עֲצָמִים in some poetry and of pieces in a pot.

senses.definition: A bone of the body, of man or beast; the hard frame under the flesh and skin, what is left in the grave when the flesh is gone.

evidence.note: “With skin and flesh you clothed me, and with עֲצָמוֹת and sinews you knit me together”: bones beside skin, flesh and sinew.
To the bones: “I will lay sinews on you and bring up flesh on you and cover you with skin.”
They tear “their flesh from off their עַצְמוֹת”; and in Mic 3:3 break their bones and chop them as for the pot.
The Passover lamb: “you shall not break a עֶצֶם in it”.
The same at the second Passover.
Whoever touches one slain, or a dead body, “or a עֶצֶם of a man, or a grave”, is unclean seven days.
Joseph: “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my עַצְמֹת from here.”
Joseph’s bones buried at Shechem.
David brings up the bones of Saul and Jonathan and buries them.
“Men’s bones shall be burned on you”, fulfilled in 2Ki 23:16.
A dead man thrown into Elisha’s grave touches Elisha’s bones and lives.
The bones of kings, priests and prophets brought out of their graves and spread before the sun.
Moab burned the bones of the king of Edom to lime.
The choicest pieces and עֲצָמִים in the cauldron.
The valley full of dry bones, which come together “bone to its bone”.
God “shall eat up the nations his adversaries and break their bones”.
Behemoth: “his עֲצָמִים are tubes of bronze”: bone as strength.
How the bones grow in the womb of her who is with child, which no one knows.
“Our bones are scattered at the mouth of Sheol”: of the grave.

senses.gloss: the bones as the body, the whole person
senses.definition: The bones as the inner frame of the whole person: what wastes in grief and sickness, shakes in fear, burns with a word held in, and is refreshed by good news and healing. Often in parallel with heart, soul or flesh.

evidence.note: “Heal me, Yahweh, for my עֲצָמַי are troubled”, beside “my soul is greatly troubled” (Psa 6:4).
“The light of the eyes rejoices the heart; good news makes fat the עָצֶם.”
Pleasant words are “sweet to the soul and healing to the עָצֶם”.
Fearing Yahweh is “healing to your navel and drink to your bones”.
“A heart of healing is life to the flesh, but envy is rottenness of the bones.”
A shameful wife is “as rottenness in his bones”.
“When I kept silent, my bones wore away through my groaning all day long”: sin unconfessed.
“My strength fails because of my iniquity, and my bones waste away.”
“There is no peace in my bones because of my sin.”
“Let the bones you have crushed rejoice.”
“All my bones shall say, Yahweh, who is like you?”: the whole self.
“All my bones are out of joint.”
“I may count all my bones; they look and stare at me.”
“My bone cleaves to my flesh”: wasted to skin and bone.
Fear “made the greater part of my bones to shake”.
Yahweh’s word “in my heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones”.
“My heart within me is broken; all my bones shake.”
“Rottenness entered my bones.”
Yahweh “will make strong your bones”.
“Your bones shall flourish like the grass.”
The Nazirites “were more ruddy in עֶצֶם than corals”: in body.
“Touch his bone and his flesh”: his own body, after his goods and children.

senses.gloss: bone and flesh: one’s own kin
senses.definition: In “my bone and my flesh”, one of the same body and blood: a near kinsman, and of the woman, one made from the man’s own body.

evidence.note: “This one at last is עֶצֶם from my עֲצָמַי and flesh from my flesh; she shall be called woman, for from man she was taken.”
Laban to Jacob, his sister’s son: “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.”
Abimelech to the men of Shechem, his mother’s kin: “remember that I am your bone and your flesh”.
All the tribes to David: “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh.”
David to the elders of Judah and to Amasa: “you are my bone and my flesh”.
“We are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones”, then Gen 2:24 (Eph 5:31): the words of Gen 2:23 applied to Christ and the ecclesia.

senses.definition: With a noun after it, the thing itself and no other: בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה “on the bone of this day”, on this very day; “as the bone of the heavens”, as the heavens themselves.

evidence.note: No bread, parched grain or fresh ear “until עֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, until you have brought the offering of your God”: the day of the עֹמֶר itself, and no earlier.
At Shavuot, the fiftieth day: “you shall proclaim on this very day a holy convocation”.
“You shall do no work on this very day, for it is Yom Kippurim, a day of coverings, to make a covering for you before Yahweh your God.”
Whoever does not humble himself “on this very day” shall be cut off.
Whoever does any work “on this very day”, Yahweh will destroy from his people.
“At the end of 430 years, on this very day, all the hosts of Yahweh went out from the land of Egypt.”
Keep the feast of Unleavened Bread, “for on this very day I brought your hosts out”.
“On this very day Noah … entered the ark”: the day just dated in Gen 7:11.
Abraham circumcised his house “on this very day, as God had said to him”.
Yahweh speaks to Moses “on this very day” to go up and die.
Israel eats of the land’s produce “on the morrow after the Passover … on this very day”.
“To this very day.”
Israel’s rebellion “to this very day”.
“Write the name of the day, this very day: the king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem on this very day.”
Under his feet “as it were a work of sapphire pavement, and as the עֶצֶם of the heavens for clearness”: the heavens themselves.
“One dies בְּעֶצֶם תֻּמּוֹ”, in his very fulness, wholly at ease and quiet.

evidence.locator: Gen.2.23, עֶצֶם → ὀστοῦν, עֲצָמַי → ὀστέων; Exo.12.46 and Num.9.12, עֶצֶם → ὀστοῦν; Ezk.37.1 the same

evidence.note: “That the scripture should be fulfilled, ὀστοῦν of him shall not be broken”: Exo 12:46; Num 9:12; Psa 34:21.
“Of his flesh and of his ὀστέων”, from Gen 2:23.
Joseph by faith “gave commandment concerning his ὀστέων” (Gen 50:25).
The risen Jesus: “a spirit has not flesh and ὀστέα, as you see me have”.
Graves full of dead men’s bones.

parallels.note: “Flesh”, beside it of the body and in “bone and flesh” of kin.
“Soul”, beside the bones as the whole person.

phrases.gloss: on this very day, on this selfsame day
until this very day; to this very day
my bone and my flesh: my own kin

words.summary: Mighty, mostly of a nation or people, and nearly always beside רַב or גָּדוֹל: great in number and strength together.

senses.gloss: mighty, strong (of a people, an army, kings)
senses.definition: Strong, too strong to be withstood; of a nation, an army or kings, usually paired with “great” or “many”.

evidence.note: Abraham “shall surely become a great and עָצוּם nation, and in him all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (quoted in Gal 3:8).
Pharaoh: “the people of the sons of Israel are more and mightier than we”.
Balak: “this people is too mighty for me; perhaps I shall be able to strike them”.
“Few in number … and there he became a nation, great, עָצוּם and many.”
Nations “greater and mightier than you” driven out.
He “slew mighty kings”.
The waters of the River, “mighty and many”: the king of Assyria.
“I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the עֲצוּמִים, because he poured out his soul to death.”
“When one stronger than he comes upon him and overcomes him, he takes his armour and divides his spoils”: the words of Isa 53:12.
“The small one shall become a strong nation.”
He will judge “strong nations far off”, and they will beat their swords into ploughshares.
The lame made a remnant and the cast off “a strong nation”, with Yahweh reigning over them in Mount Zion.
“Many peoples and strong nations shall come to seek Yahweh of hosts in Jerusalem.”
A nation “strong and without number”: the locusts.
“Strong is he who does his word.”
He shall destroy “the mighty ones and the people of the holy ones”.
The lot parts between “the mighty”: strong contenders.
The rock badgers are “a people not עָצוּם”, yet house themselves in the rock.
The helpless fall “by his strong ones”: the wicked man’s claws or his men.

senses.definition: Many in number, where the stress is on how many: livestock, a congregation, the slain, sins.

evidence.note: “The sons of Reuben and Gad had very much livestock, עָצוּם מְאֹד.”
“I will thank you in the great congregation; I will praise you among a numerous people”: parallel to קָהָל רָב.
“Many are the slain she has cast down, and numerous all her slain.”
“I know how many (רַבִּים) are your transgressions and how numerous your sins.”

evidence.locator: Isa.53.12, עֲצוּמִים → ἰσχυρῶν; ἰσχυρός renders עָצוּם ×11

evidence.note: “When ὁ ἰσχυρός, armed, guards his house … when one ἰσχυρότερος than he comes … he divides his spoils”: Isa 53:12’s dividing the spoil with the עֲצוּמִים.

parallels.note: “Many”, beside it of nations, peoples and sins.

opposites.note: “Few”: Israel went down few and became mighty.
“The small one” made a strong nation.

words.gloss: be mighty, numerous; make strong; shut the eyes; break the bones
words.summary: Most of its uses are “be mighty” and “be many”, the two together in a people that multiplies (Exo 1:7). Twice it is “shut the eyes” (Isa 29:10; 33:15), whose tie to the root is not clear, and once, in the piel, “break the bones” (Jer 50:17), a verb made from עֶצֶם.

stems.gloss: be mighty, strong; be numerous; shut (the eyes)

senses.definition: To be or grow strong, often with מִן, “stronger than”: of a man, a people, a ruler or an enemy.

evidence.note: Abimelech to Isaac: “Go from us, for you are much mightier than we.”
“The sons of Israel were fruitful and swarmed and multiplied and grew mighty, very very much, and the land was filled with them.”
“The people multiplied and grew very mighty.”
“His power shall be mighty (וְעָצַם כֹּחוֹ), but not by his own power.”
“When he was strong, the great horn was broken.”
He “shall become strong with a small people”.
“My enemies are lively, they are strong (עָצֵמוּ), and many (רַבּוּ) are they who hate me wrongfully.”
“Mighty are they who would destroy me.”
Those who trust in horsemen “because they are very strong”.

senses.gloss: be numerous, be more than can be counted
senses.definition: To be many, more than can be told or numbered; of sins, widows, God’s thoughts and works.

evidence.note: “If I would declare and speak of them, they are more (עָצְמוּ) than can be numbered.”
“Evils without number … they are more than the hairs of my head.”
“How precious are your thoughts to me, O God! How great is the sum of them!”
“Their widows are more to me than the sand of the seas.”
“Their transgressions are many (רַבּוּ), their backslidings numerous (עָצְמוּ).”
“Because of the greatness of your iniquity, your sins are numerous.”

senses.definition: To close the eyes so as not to see; once, of the righteous man who will not look on evil.

evidence.note: He who “stops his ears from hearing of blood, and shuts (עֹצֵם) his eyes from looking on evil”: beside אֹטֵם, “stops” the ear.

stems.gloss: shut (the eyes) tight; break the bones

senses.definition: To shut another’s eyes, of Yahweh closing the eyes of the prophets so that they do not see.

evidence.note: “Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has shut your eyes, the prophets, and covered your heads, the seers.”
“God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see”: Isa 29:10 with Deu 29:4, of Israel’s present blindness.

senses.gloss: break the bones of, gnaw to the bone
senses.definition: To break or crunch the bones, as a lion does its prey: a verb made from עֶצֶם.

evidence.note: “Israel is a scattered sheep; lions have driven him away: first the king of Assyria devoured him, and last Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has broken his bones (עִצְּמוֹ).”

senses.definition: To make a people mighty, stronger than its foes; of God with Israel in Egypt.

evidence.note: “He increased his people greatly, and made them stronger than their adversaries”: Exo 1:7 told as God’s doing.

evidence.locator: Isa.33.15, עֹצֵם → καμμύων; Isa.29.10, יְעַצֵּם → καμμύσει

evidence.note: “Their eyes they have closed (ἐκάμμυσαν)”, quoting Isa 6:10 in the Septuagint’s words, where the Hebrew verb is another (הָשַׁע): the bridge from Isa 29:10’s closed eyes to the New Testament’s.

parallels.note: “Multiply, be many”, beside it of Israel in Egypt, enemies and sins.

words.summary: Only three times: twice “the might of the hand”, once “my frame”, the body’s bones being formed in the womb. The one word holds both halves of the root.

senses.definition: The strength of a hand that does or strikes: a man’s, which he must not credit with his wealth, and God’s.

evidence.note: “Lest you say in your heart, My power (כֹּחִי) and the might of my hand (עֹצֶם יָדִי) has got me this wealth”; Deu 8:18: it is Yahweh who gives power to get wealth.
“With the might of your hand you oppose me.”

senses.definition: The body’s frame of bones, as it is formed before birth.

evidence.note: “My frame (עָצְמִי) was not hidden from you when I was made in secret, skilfully wrought in the depths of the earth.”

senses.definition: Strength that God gives to the weary; the strength of a city in its allies; the great force of spells.

evidence.note: “He gives power (כֹּחַ) to the faint, and to him who has no might (אוֹנִים) he increases עָצְמָה.”
To Babylon: loss of children and widowhood will come “in spite of the great strength of your enchantments”.
To Nineveh, of No-amon: “Cush and Egypt were her strength, and it was without end; Put and Lubim were your helpers.”

words.summary: Once, in the plural, of the power God gives his people.

senses.definition: Power that God gives his people, beside עֹז, strength.

evidence.note: “The God of Israel, he gives strength (עֹז) and power (תַעֲצֻמוֹת) to the people. Blessed be God!”

words.summary: Once, in the plural with a suffix: what the idols’ worshippers are told to bring to court. It is formed like the passive עָצוּם, “strong”, so “your strong (points)”: the case they think strong. Its tie to the root is through that sense of strength; nothing else confirms it.

senses.gloss: strong argument, one’s strong points in a case
senses.definition: In a lawsuit, what each side brings forward as its strength.

evidence.note: “Bring near your case (רִיבְכֶם), says Yahweh; bring forth your strong arguments (עֲצֻמוֹתֵיכֶם), says the King of Jacob”: parallel to רִיב, a lawsuit, against the idols (Isa 41:22–24).

cognates.gloss: bone (of an animal, on which is the flesh); pl. ʿiẓām
cognates.note: The same root as ʿaẓuma “be great”: Lane’s sources say the verb “primarily signifies he was, or became, great in his bone”, then great in anything. Form II ʿaẓẓama also means “cut up the sheep bone by bone”. Arabic ظ (ẓ) shows ṯ̣ behind צ.

evidence.note: “He cut up the sheep, or goat, bone by bone.”

cognates.gloss: be or become great, big; great, mighty, of great account
cognates.note: “He was, or became, great in his bone: then metaphorically said of anything great”; ʿaẓīm “great … in comparison with other things of its kind”, of men and “in an incomparably higher sense, of God”; muʿẓam “the greater, main part” and ʿuẓm “a numerous company”. Greatness, might and number together, as in עָצַם and עָצוּם; and the same ẓ (ṯ̣) as ʿaẓm “bone”, so one older root.

evidence.note: “The greater, main … part”; عُظْمٌ “a numerous company”.

cognates.note: Vocalised /ʿaẓm-/. Ugaritic ẓ, like Arabic, shows ṯ̣ behind צ.
Akkadian ṣ does not show which older sound stands behind צ.
On coffins and tombstones: “do not open this resting-place nor disturb my bones” (KAI 9 A 5); “here in this place have her bones been gathered”.

evidence.locator: p. 384, ʿṢM, pl. ʿṢMM, n.m. BONE; KAI 9 A 5, RES 937

cognates.note: Eshmunazor of Sidon: the Lord of Kings gave Dor and Joppa “as a reward for the great deeds (ʿṣmt) that I accomplished” (KAI 14.18–19). Might shown in what is done, as עֹצֶם יָדִי (Deu 8:17), beside ʿṣm “bone” in the same language.

evidence.locator: p. 384, ʿṢMT, n.f. GREAT DEED; KAI 14.18/19

cognates.note: Neo-Punic: “possessor of a crown and possessor of a reputation (šm) for mighty deeds (tʿṣmt)” (KAI 165.6–7). The same formation as תַּעֲצֻמָה.

evidence.locator: p. 467, ŠM III 2, KAI 165.6/7 (NPu) šm tʿṣmt

cognates.note: Not yet checked in Dillmann or Leslau, so no sound is recorded: Ge’ez manuscripts write ጸ (ṣ) and ፀ (ḍ) for each other, and the spelling here does not settle ṣ́ against ṯ̣.

Jewish Aramaic, = אַטְמָא “flank” (Targ. II Esth. 1:2; Y. Meg. I, 70d). Aramaic ṭ answers to Arabic ẓ (ṯ̣), so the sound fits Hebrew עֶצֶם; the meaning is a part of the body, not bone, so it is recorded as possible. The Targums’ usual word for bone is גַּרְמָא.

“He shut, or closed, his eyes, or his eyelids”; mā ʾaġmaḍtu “I have not slept”. The root is ġ-m-ḍ, with the second and third letters the other way round from עצם, so this is a lead for “shut the eyes”, not proof; if it holds, ġ and ṣ́ (ḍ) stand behind ע and צ here, against ʿ and ṯ̣ in ʿaẓm “bone”: another older root in the same spelling.

Jewish Aramaic, “he closed and opened his eyes” (Bets. 22a); Hebrew of the Mishnah has מְעַמְּצִין and מְעַצְּמִין side by side for closing a dead man’s eyes (Sabb. 23:5), so עמץ and עצם interchange in this sense. Like Arabic ġmḍ, it has the letters in another order.

evidence.locator: s.v. עֲמַץ (P00916); s.v. עָמַץ, Pi. (Sabb. XXIII, 5)

doctrine.statement: Lev 23 fixes its feasts not to a season but to “this very day” (בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה): the new harvest is not to be eaten until the very day the עֹמֶר is brought (Lev 23:14); the fiftieth day is proclaimed holy on that day (Lev 23:21); and on Yom Kippurim, the day of coverings, whoever works or does not humble himself “on this very day” is cut off (Lev 23:28–30). The same words are used of what God did: the flood came and Noah entered the ark “on this very day” (Gen 7:11–13), and “at the end of 430 years, on this very day, all the hosts of Yahweh went out from Egypt” (Exo 12:41), which is why the feast of Unleavened Bread is kept on its day (Exo 12:17). From the verses: the appointed days are kept to the day because God acted to the day; his times are not approximate, and his people’s keeping of them answers his exactness.

Of the Passover lamb the law says twice, “you shall not break a bone (עֶצֶם) of it” (Exo 12:46; Num 9:12), and a psalm says of the righteous man, “he keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken” (Psa 34:20–21). When the soldiers broke the legs of the two crucified with Jesus but found him already dead, they did not break his; John says “these things were done that the scripture should be fulfilled, a bone of him shall not be broken” (Jhn 19:32–36). From the verses: the lamb whose blood saved Israel’s firstborn was a figure of Jesus, and even this detail of its eating was written for him; Paul says the same plainly, “Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us” (1Co 5:7).

The bones are what the grave keeps of a man (Num 19:16; Jer 8:1; Psa 141:7). In Ezekiel’s vision the bones are “very dry”, and life does not come by any part of them surviving: God lays sinews, flesh and skin on them and puts breath in them, “and you shall live” (Ezk 37:1–10). He explains it as Israel saying “our bones are dried up and our hope is lost”, answered by “I will open your graves and cause you to come up out of your graves, my people, and bring you into the land of Israel” (Ezk 37:11–12). A dead man touching Elisha’s bones “lived and stood up on his feet” (2Ki 13:21); and the risen Jesus showed that he was no spirit, for “a spirit has not flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luk 24:39). From the verses: the hope of the dead is not a soul living on apart from the bones but a body raised from the grave by God’s breath, and the nation’s restoration to its land is told in the same terms.

Joseph, dying in Egypt, said “I am dying, but God will surely visit you and bring you up out of this land to the land he swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob”, and made Israel swear to carry up his bones (Gen 50:24–25). Moses took them at the exodus (Exo 13:19), and they were buried at Shechem in the land (Jos 24:32). Hebrews counts it as faith: “by faith Joseph, when he was dying, made mention of the going out of the sons of Israel and gave commandment concerning his bones” (Heb 11:22), among those who “died in faith, not having received the promises” (Heb 11:13). From the verses: Joseph’s hope was in the promise of the land to the fathers, and he wanted his bones there to await it.

The woman was built from a part taken out of the man, and he said, “This one at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen 2:21–23); “therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and they shall be one flesh” (Gen 2:24). Elsewhere “my bone and my flesh” names a man’s own kin (Gen 29:14; 2Sa 5:1). Paul applies Genesis to Christ and the ecclesia: “we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones; for this cause a man shall leave his father and mother … this is a great mystery, but I speak concerning Christ and the ecclesia” (Eph 5:30–32). From the verses: a wife is her husband’s own body, as near as kin can be, and the ecclesia is Christ’s in the same way.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13 for Lev 23:14, 21, 28–30. Root key עצמ as the corpus keys it. BDB keys: p.eq.aa and p.er.aa are the same 20 verb tokens in the database (BDB splits “be mighty” from “shut the eyes” but the text files every token under both), so the verb takes p.eq.aa only and p.er.aa is left unclaimed; p.es.aa is a root heading with no tokens and w.bi.ac a cross-reference with no tokens. Left out: the place names עֶצֶם Ezem (p.eq.ae; Jos 15:29; 19:3; 1Ch 4:29) and עַצְמוֹן Azmon (p.eq.ah; Num 34:4–5; Jos 15:4), which are places and so cannot be name entries. עֲצֻמָה (p.es.ab, Isa 41:21) is kept as “strong arguments” from עָצוּם; the rendering is from the parallel רִיב and its formation, with no cognate. Open questions: (1) “Shut the eyes” (Isa 29:10; 33:15) rests only on possible cognates with the letters in another order (Arabic ġmḍ, Aramaic עמץ); if they hold, it is a second older root (ġ, ṣ́) in this spelling. (2) The “very, selfsame” use is taken as bone > the thing itself; no cognate uses the bone word that way in the sources checked. (3) Lam 4:7 עֶצֶם is read as “body” (ruddy in body); it could be “bone” in the sense of complexion. Leads not followed: Syriac ܥܰܛܡܳܐ “thigh” (Payne Smith not checked; the Peshitta New Testament has no word of this root in SEDRA); Ugaritic ʿṣm “strong” (Wiktionary only; not in Segert or Fisher); Ge’ez ʿaḍm in Dillmann and Leslau; Old South Arabian. Thayer’s ἰσχυρός from עָצוּם is a Septuagint rendering, not a loan.
